title: Character Before Competence: A Church Leadership Study
subtitle: A five-session study on leading the church without losing your soul.
summary:
This study is for pastors, elders, deacons, and the teams who carry a church together. It's also for anyone who has felt the distance between the person the work demands and the person they actually are. Over five sessions it looks at what God actually screens for in a leader, at the inner life and the exhaustion nobody sees, at the idol of being needed, at who you put in the room and why nobody is safe to lead alone, and at the three things that have brought down most of the leaders we've lost, along with the last work of raising the person who comes after you. A busy leadership team can run it with little preparation. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than strategy.

It isn't a study that lets the gifted off the hook because the numbers are good, and it isn't a study that looks down on skill. Someone who can't teach shouldn't be appointed to teach, and a treasurer who can't read a balance sheet is a liability, however willing. The argument is about order. Character is the foundation and competence is the house built on it. I'm not writing from outside this. Leaders like me run the searches that let a bright gift do the screening character should have done, handle holy things all week without being fed by them, and build ministries that can't run without us. Those are my dangers too, and the study asks every leader at the table to read it as a mirror.
audience: Pastors, elders, deacons, and leadership teams

sessions.title: Almost All Character
sessions.aim: To read God's two lists for a leader the right way up again: almost everything on them describes who a person is, and very little describes what a person can do. And to refuse both the church that hires on the résumé and the false piety that pretends skill doesn't matter.
sessions.summary:
The New Testament gives us two lists of what to look for in a leader, one in Paul's letter to Timothy and one in his letter to Titus, and the church has often read them upside down. Count what they name: above reproach, faithful in marriage, sober-minded, self-controlled, gentle, not violent, not greedy, not a lover of money, managing his own household well. The one item that is plainly a skill is "able to teach" (1 Timothy 3:2). Nearly everything else describes the person when no crowd is watching.

Two answers pull against each other here. One says character is everything and competence is worldly. It's right that God screens almost entirely for the person under the gift. The other says skill matters, and it's right too, because the lists themselves include the ability to teach. The point isn't that competence is wicked or that the résumé is enough. It's order. Gifts show up early and character grows slowly, so we tend to reward what we can see arriving. And the list names the home as the proving ground, because the way someone leads where nobody is watching is the way they'll lead everywhere once the watching stops.

keyScripture.why: "Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money" (1 Timothy 3:2-3). Almost every line is about character, and the single skill, able to teach, sits in the middle of a list about self-government. God is screening the person, not the résumé.

discussion.q: Think about the last time you helped choose a leader, or were chosen as one. What did the choosing actually weigh? What did that cost, then or later?
discussion.behind: Bring the habit into the open before teaching anything. Most leadership teams screen for what's easy to see, because competence is easy to measure and character isn't. You aren't settling anything yet. Go first if the room is slow; you've probably run that kind of search yourself.

discussion.q: Read 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 1:5-9 aloud. Make two columns, things about who a person is and things about what a person can do. What do you notice when you're finished?
discussion.behind: Let the room do the counting. The second column will be very short, with "able to teach" the clear entry and perhaps a debate over "hospitable" or managing a household. That debate is fine. The point is how lopsided the lists are, and that God could have asked mostly about talent and didn't.

discussion.q: Gifts tend to show up early and wisdom tends to show up late. Where have you seen someone's gift rewarded long before the person under it had grown into it?
discussion.behind: Keep this on the mechanism, not on gossip about particular people. A sermon can be judged in twelve minutes; a life takes years. We reward the fast thing because the slow thing is hard to see. If names start coming up, steer gently back to the pattern.

discussion.q: Paul asks, "if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?" (1 Timothy 3:5). Why would Scripture treat the private life as the evidence and the public life as the footnote?
discussion.behind: The home is where the unpolished version of us lives, and the unpolished version is the real one. Be tender here. Someone at the table has a hard marriage or a struggling child, and the verse isn't a demand for a trouble-free family. It asks whether the private life supports the public one.

discussion.q: Where have you let a bright gift do the discerning for you, in choosing someone else or in judging yourself?
discussion.behind: Turn the question inward and answer it first, briefly and truly. You're not after a confession that shames anyone. You want each person, you included, to see that we've all read the lists upside down at some point.

objections.objection: Character talk is an excuse for incompetence. The work is hard and the stakes are real. A kind, godly person who can't preach, can't run a meeting, or can't read a budget will sink a church no matter how good his marriage is.
objections.response: Most of that is true, and it's worth saying plainly. Competence isn't wicked. Someone who can't teach shouldn't be appointed to teach, and a church that despised skill would be foolish in its own way. Paul himself put "able to teach" on the list. But the question isn't whether competence matters. It's which comes first. Character is the foundation and competence is the house, and a house without a foundation isn't a bargain. It's a delay. The gifted leader whose character never grew under the gift doesn't save the church trouble. He postpones it, and the bill tends to arrive all at once, on a day that looks sudden only to the people who were watching the skill and not the soul. Build the foundation first, then build the house on it.

objections.objection: By this standard nobody is qualified, including the people teaching the study. If we wait for flawless character we'll never appoint anyone and the work won't get done.
objections.response: That's a real danger, and the lists don't ask for sinlessness. A church that waits for a perfect leader will appoint no one. "Above reproach" doesn't mean above sin. It means there's no unaddressed pattern of the kind that wrecks a flock: no ongoing affair, no hidden theft, no temper the household lives in fear of. Still, the lists do screen, and they screen for things that grow slowly and hide easily. The answer to a high bar isn't to lower it to the résumé. It's to start forming character on purpose, years before anyone is appointed, so that when the moment comes there are people whose souls have grown under their gifts. The standard isn't perfection. It's a foundation deep enough to hold what the storm will one day put on it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Of the places where trouble usually starts, money, temper, appetite, the home, which would show first if someone examined you tonight the way Paul examines an overseer?
sessions.practice: This week, read the two lists slowly, 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 1:5-9, with your own name in mind rather than someone else's. Don't treat them as a hiring checklist. Write down the one line that lands hardest, the place where your gift may be running ahead of your character. Then ask what that gap is quietly costing, and what it would take to start closing it now. Don't grade the answer; just write it down.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you look at the heart, and we look at the résumé, and we've done it so long we hardly notice. We've rewarded the gift and ignored the person under it, in others and in ourselves, and called our hurry discernment. Forgive us, and forgive your church for the collapses it never saw coming because it was watching the wrong things. Teach us to weigh what you weigh, to lay the foundation before we build the house, and to grow the character the hard days will ask of us. Do your slow work in us where no one is watching. Amen.
reflection: The last time I helped choose a leader, or was chosen, what did we actually weigh, and what did that cost the church and me?
Where in my own life is the gift running ahead of the person under it?
If the home is where the real version of me shows, what does my unwatched leadership reveal that my Sunday leadership hides?
sessions.teaching:
Let's start with two lists. The New Testament has two places where Paul tells a younger leader what to look for in an overseer, and I think the church has often read them upside down. Here's the first: "Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money" (1 Timothy 3:2-3). And here's the same office on Crete: "For an overseer, as God's steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined" (Titus 1:7-8).

Now count. The one item that is plainly a skill is "able to teach," and Titus repeats it in a different form when Paul says the elder must be able to give instruction in sound doctrine (Titus 1:9). Nearly everything else describes the person when no crowd is forming: what he does with money and anger and appetite, how he treats the people who've seen him at his worst, how his home feels to live in. God could have built his church on raw talent. Instead, when he named what to look for in the people who would carry it, he asked almost entirely about who they are when the lights are off.

There are two answers here, and each has hold of something true. The first says character is everything and competence is a worldly distraction. It's right about the lists. Dallas Willard spent much of his life arguing that the church has treated becoming like Christ as optional, and that we've produced leaders who can perform the Christian life at a high level without being much changed by it. The second answer says skill matters too. Someone who can't teach shouldn't teach, and a treasurer who can't read a balance sheet is a liability, however willing. That's right as well, and the lists themselves say so.

So the point isn't that competence is wicked, and it isn't that the résumé is enough. It's order. Character is the foundation and competence is the house. A house without a foundation isn't a bargain. It's a delay. And the reason we keep getting the order wrong isn't mysterious. Gifts show up fast. A person can be more talented at thirty than he'll be wise at sixty. Talent appears early, gets rewarded early, and earns the stage early, so we learn to look for the thing we can see arriving. A sermon can be judged in twelve minutes. A character takes twelve years.

I've been in the room where this happens, and I suspect you have too. We sit across from a gifted candidate and let the gift do the screening that character should have done, and we tell ourselves we're being strategic. Usually we're being lazy. We measure what's easy and call it discernment. The distance between God's list and ours is the same distance we later discover when a leader collapses and everyone says they never saw it coming. We didn't see it because we were watching what God barely weighed and ignoring what he weighed most.

Then there's the line we skip fastest. "He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?" (1 Timothy 3:4-5). That's not a nice principle; it holds up the whole list. The home is where every kind of authority gets rehearsed, and the way someone leads where he's least watched is the way he'll lead where he's most watched once the watching stops. Sunday is the polished version. Home is the unpolished one, and the unpolished one is the real one. We treat the public life as the evidence and the private life as a footnote. Scripture does the reverse. That doesn't mean a leader's family must be free of trouble; no parent can promise how a child will turn out. It means the private life has to support the public claim.

Paul had watched churches built and broken in real cities, and he knew where the trouble usually started: marriage, temper, appetite, money. So he wrote a hiring rubric that is almost entirely a character interview, and not one line of it asks how full the room gets when the man speaks. God made the same point long before, when Samuel looked at Jesse's impressive sons and was told, "man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7).

If this session makes you uneasy about how you last chose a leader, or about how you'd fare if someone examined you the same way, don't hear that unease as condemnation. It's mercy arriving early, while there's still time to grow what the storm will one day test.

scriptureStudy.note: "Above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money." Notice how much of the list concerns appetite, temper, and money, and how little concerns ability.
"If someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?" The home is named as the proof. The public office rests on the private life, not the other way round.

The same office on Crete and the same weighting: "not arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined." A second witness that God screens the person.

The elder "must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine." The teaching gift matters, and even here it's tied to faithfulness to the word rather than to talent on its own.

"For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart." God passes over Jesse's impressive sons for the youngest. The pattern of the two lists is already here.
The wise man builds on rock and the foolish man on sand, and only the storm shows the difference. Competence without character is a house that stands fine until the weather comes.
"Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching." Paul names the self first and the teaching second, the order of this whole study.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a team that wants to go further, take up the old argument over whether character can be assessed at all, because the habit of screening the résumé is partly an honest surrender to how hard the alternative is. The moral tradition that runs from Aristotle, through Augustine and later Aquinas, understood virtue as a settled habit formed slowly, in repeated action and mostly out of sight. That's exactly the thing a search committee can't measure in an afternoon. A recording of a sermon can be watched in twelve minutes. A virtue takes years to form and years more to verify, so an institution under pressure to fill a pulpit reaches for what it can see.

Set that beside Willard's complaint that the church has made formation optional, and ask whether our hiring habits are a cause of that or a symptom of it. Both things are true: character really is hard to assess, and the difficulty has become an excuse to stop trying. The way out isn't resignation. It's building patient, mostly hidden formation into the life of the church long before an appointment is on the table, so that when the moment comes the committee isn't forced to choose between a flawless stranger and a gifted risk.

sessions.title: Handling Is Not Eating
sessions.aim: To name a strange danger in ministry: you can handle the things of God all week and still go hungry. And to see that the inner life, and the exhaustion no one sees, aren't weaknesses to hide but the foundation everything visible rests on.
sessions.summary:
You can starve at a feast if your job is carrying the plates. That's one of the strangest dangers in church leadership, and almost nobody warns you about it. You study the text, teach it, counsel from it, and pray at the graveside, and it's entirely possible to do all of it without being fed by any of it. Handling isn't eating.

Two pressures pull against each other. One says the work itself is devotion, and the work is good and given by God. The other says the inner life is a luxury a busy leader can't afford, because prayer produces nothing you can report and the needs are real. Acts 6 answers both. The widows really were being overlooked, and the apostles didn't ignore them. They built a structure to feed them well, and then they guarded prayer and the ministry of the word on purpose. Guarding the inner life usually means defending it against good things, not bad ones. The exhaustion that ends a ministry is often less about doing too much than about doing it from a soul that's never been fed.

keyScripture.why: "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. ... But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:2, 4). Facing a real need, the apostles build a structure that meets it well and still defend the one thing only they can do. Guarding the inner life means guarding it against good things.

discussion.q: When did you last read Scripture or pray simply as a hungry person, for your own soul, with no one to teach it to and nothing to produce from it?
discussion.behind: Start with recognition, not guilt. Many people in leadership read the Bible professionally, looking for what they can use. From the outside that looks exactly like devotion, which is why the hunger goes unnoticed. Go first.

discussion.q: Read Acts 6:1-7. What was the problem, how did the apostles answer it, and what did their answer cost them?
discussion.behind: Make sure the room sees both halves. The widows' need was real and the apostles met it, through seven men "full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). They also disappointed people who wanted more of them. Notice too that the word "increased" in verse 7 comes after the decision, not before it.

discussion.q: People often say you don't rise to the occasion, you fall to your training. Where have you assumed the public moments form you, when it's really the hidden years that do?
discussion.behind: The crisis usually reveals what the ordinary days have already built. Help the room see that the formation that matters is happening now, in unremarkable weeks, not in the big moments they're bracing for.

discussion.q: What good and genuine thing is crowding out the one or two things only you can do?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. Don't let it turn into a complaint about being busy. The needs crowding out prayer aren't temptations. They're real people with real wounds. That's exactly why they're hard to say no to.

discussion.q: Paul says, "we have this treasure in jars of clay" (2 Corinthians 4:7). If the jar has to be filled before it can carry anything, how would you know whether you're being filled or only running dry?
discussion.behind: We usually hear "jars of clay" as comfort about weakness, and it is. But the treasure is inside the jar. Help the room name the signs of running dry before the day it cracks, and turn the question on yourself first.

objections.objection: Guarding your inner life while real people have real needs is self-indulgence dressed up as spirituality. The widows were actually going hungry. A leader who retreats to pray while people are hurting is neglecting the very people he was called to serve.
objections.response: The needs are real, and that deserves to be said first. The widows in Acts 6 were among the most vulnerable people in that society, the people God's law repeatedly commands his people to protect, and they were being overlooked. A leader who hides behind prayer to avoid people he's called to love hasn't guarded his soul. He's abandoned his post. But look at what the apostles actually did. They didn't ignore the widows. They had seven men chosen, "of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3), so the need was met and met well. Then they defended the one thing only they could do. That's the pattern: build the structure so people are cared for, and guard the prayer, because a leader who serves every table and never feeds his own soul will eventually have nothing left for the people he's protecting.

objections.objection: Plenty of faithful leaders are too busy for long quiet times and they're doing fine. Some of us are in seasons where the work simply doesn't allow it, and we trust God to sustain us in the doing.
objections.response: Seasons are real, and God does carry people through brutal stretches. There are weeks when the work crowds out nearly everything, and getting through them on grace and very little sleep isn't faithlessness. But a season is different from a way of life. When leaders give up the work, it isn't always because the work got harder, though it often did. Sometimes it's because the work hollowed them out and there was nothing underneath to draw on. The output can look fine for years, which is exactly what makes this dangerous. A season of running dry is survivable. A ministry built on the assumption that the doing will feed you is a jar headed for the heat. Honor the hard seasons, and don't build your whole life out of them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Is there a person under your public role, formed in the hidden years, or mostly a surface carrying bread to others while you go hungry? How would you know before it cracks?
sessions.practice: This week, before you prepare anything for anyone else, sit with one passage as a hungry person. No one else is in the room and nothing has to come of it. Let it find the place in your own life it's aiming at, and don't move on to how you'd use it. Then, separately, name the one good thing that most reliably crowds out what only you can do, and decide on purpose to protect the essential from it this week, even if that disappoints someone who has every right to want more of you. Write down what it cost.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've handled holy things all week and gone hungry. We've carried bread to everyone else and hardly tasted it, and we've called that devotion because our hands were full. Forgive us for serving every table and neglecting our own souls. Teach us to eat before we serve, to guard our prayer against the many good things that would bury it, and to be jars you have filled. You put your treasure in clay on purpose, so that the power would be seen to be yours. Fill us in the hidden hours, before the day we crack. Amen.
reflection: When did I last read Scripture or pray for my own soul, with nothing to produce from it?
What good thing is crowding out what only I can do, and what would it cost to protect the essential this week?
What are the signs in me of running dry, and who would notice them before I did?
sessions.teaching:
You can starve at a feast if your job is carrying the plates. That's one of the strangest dangers in leadership, and almost nobody warns you about it until it's already begun. You handle the things of God all week. You study the text, teach it, counsel from it, pray over meals and over the dying and at the open grave. Your hands are in holy things from Monday to Sunday. And it's entirely possible to do all of it without eating a bite, to carry the bread to everyone else and never taste it yourself. The waiter isn't fed by the meal he serves.

Many pastors learn the difference only after living a long time on the wrong side of it. They prepare sermons they don't let preach to them. They read Scripture professionally, looking for what they can use on Sunday, and lose the older habit of reading it as a hungry person reads, for their own soul. From the outside it looks exactly like devotion, which is why nobody notices, including them.

Two pressures pull against each other here. The first says the work is the feeding, that someone whose whole week is spent in holy things must be nourished by them. There's truth in that; the work is good, and God gave it. The second says the inner life is a luxury a busy leader can't afford. Prayer and unhurried reading produce nothing you can report, and the needs pressing in are real. That's true too. But handling still isn't eating, and you can be surrounded by holy things and slowly starve inside them.

The first leadership crisis in the church shows the way through. In Acts 6 the Greek-speaking widows "were being neglected in the daily distribution" (Acts 6:1). The complaint is fair, and the apostles answer with something that can sound almost cold: "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables" (Acts 6:2). The need was legitimate. These were among the most vulnerable people in that world. But the apostles didn't ignore them. They had the church choose seven men "full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3), and the widows were cared for well. Then they said, "we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:4). There was something only they could do, a crowd of legitimate needs would have buried it, and so they defended it on purpose and disappointed people who had every right to want more of them. Luke adds that "the word of God continued to increase" (Acts 6:7).

That's the cost nobody warns you about. Guarding your inner life usually isn't a fight against sin. It's a fight against good things. The needs that crowd out prayer aren't temptations. They're real people with real wounds asking for real help, and you could spend your whole life answering them without ever praying the prayer that holds everything up. Most of us lose that fight more often than we win it. I tell myself the meeting was ministry, the email was care, the next fire was the Lord's work, and I look up at the end of a week to find I've served every table in the building and given myself to nothing. It's easy to call that faithfulness. Often it's avoidance, because tables are visible and prayer isn't.

Eugene Peterson spent much of his life trying to get pastors to see this. In Working the Angles he complained that American pastors had turned into shopkeepers, and the shops they kept were churches, busy keeping the customers happy. He wanted pastors to recover the unhurried, hidden work no one measures: prayer, Scripture, and the kind of attention to God and to people that doesn't produce anything you can report. A leader who only handles holy things is running a life he's stopped living.

Paul gives us the image that holds all this together. "But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us" (2 Corinthians 4:7). Not a vault, but a clay pot, cheap and easily broken, chosen on purpose so that no one could mistake where the power came from. That's a real comfort to weak people. But notice that the treasure is inside the jar. A jar that carries water to others while it's bone dry isn't humble. It's empty, and in the heat it cracks, and the cracking looks sudden to everyone who didn't know.

Jesus kept this rhythm himself. "And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed" (Mark 1:35). A whole town was looking for him. He went anyway. So the question the hidden years are asking isn't whether you can handle the things of God. You clearly can. It's whether you're being fed. Carry the bread, because that's the work. But eat first.

scriptureStudy.note: "We will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word." The apostles protect what only they can do, and they do it by making sure the widows are fed, not by ignoring them.

"But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us." The jar is chosen for its weakness, but the treasure is inside it, so the jar still has to be filled.
"Abide in me, and I in you. ... for apart from me you can do nothing." Fruit is what people see. Abiding is the hidden feeding underneath it.
"On his law he meditates day and night. He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season." The roots drink where no one sees, and the fruit comes from the drinking.
"Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary." Martha's serving isn't condemned, but it isn't allowed to crowd out sitting at Jesus' feet.
"And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed." The most sought-after man in Capernaum guarded an hour no one saw.
"Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching." A leader can watch the teaching closely for years while the self Paul names first empties out behind it.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a team that wants more, look at the Desert Fathers. In the fourth century, men and women went out into the deserts of Egypt and Syria in order to be unwatched, convinced that a soul can't be formed in front of a crowd. Antony went into the desert for years. The sayings that survive from those communities aren't about technique or reach. They're about the heart in the dark. When a brother asked Abba Moses for a word, he told him, in substance, to go and sit in his cell, because the cell would teach him everything. He meant that you can't outrun yourself, and that formation happens in the plain, unwitnessed staying put.

We've built ministries around never sitting in the cell. Set the desert beside Peterson's picture of pastors turned shopkeepers, and ask whether stillness and hiddenness aren't exactly what busy leaders most need and most avoid. The desert tradition has real dangers too: escapism, a piety that walks away from people, and solitude turned into its own idol. Nobody is being asked to move to a literal desert. The aim is to build something like a cell into an ordinary week, an unwatched and unproductive hour where the soul is fed.
